fable-5.1.text:
Yeah. So I'll say this. I think my views have changed on this.

When we started, the thinking was something like: you go into the mountains, you build the thing, and when it's ready and safe, you come out and you release it. A straight shot. And the appeal of that was that you don't participate in the rat race. You're not forced to ship every few months because a competitor shipped. You get to actually think.

But I've come to believe that gradual deployment matters more than I appreciated. And the reason is pretty simple. It's very hard to imagine the world dealing well with a superintelligence that just appears. People don't respond to arguments about what an AI could do. They respond to what the AI does. When they can feel it, when they can use it, when a government can see with its own eyes that the thing is powerful, then they start to care. And I think ultimately the most important safety mechanism is that people care. That companies care, that governments care, that the public cares. You can't produce that by publishing a paper. You produce it by showing people the AI, bit by bit, as it gets stronger.

There's a second reason too, which is that if you build something in isolation, it's shaped by the imagination of the people who built it. And your imagination is always a little bit wrong. When the system is out in the world, the world tells you what you got wrong. You learn things you would not have learned otherwise. So there's a kind of humility argument for releasing incrementally as well.

So how does it fit with building superintelligence directly? I think the straight shot becomes less straight. The core idea still holds, which is that you should be doing the research without the pressure that forces you to cut corners, and you should be aiming at the thing itself rather than at the next product. But I now think that along the way you want to release systems that let people see where things are going. Not to make money, or not primarily, but so that when the really powerful systems arrive, nobody is surprised. The world has had time to adjust, to build institutions, to form opinions. I think that's much better than a sudden arrival, even if the sudden arrival were done carefully.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that even while aiming directly at superintelligence, systems should be released along the way as they get stronger.

opus-5.5.text:
I think even in the scenario where you go for the straight shot, you would still end up releasing it gradually. That's how I see it. Gradual deployment is an inherent part of any plan. The question is only what the first thing you put out the door is.

Part of the reason is that it's very hard to imagine what these systems will actually be like. You can talk about it and write essays, but until you see it and it's in the world, you don't really feel it. People struggle to internalize the power of something that doesn't exist yet. When AI starts to feel powerful, I think a lot of behavior will change. Companies will become much more concerned about safety. Governments and the public will want to do things. All of that depends on people actually seeing the AI. So showing it to the world matters a great deal.

There's another, more technical reason. When people say "AGI," they often picture a finished system that already knows how to do every job. But a human being isn't like that either. A person has some foundation, and then they go out into the world and learn. The thing you'd build is maybe more like a very capable mind that can learn to do any job. Then deployment is not only a release. It's also a period where the system learns, you see what it does, you see what goes wrong, and you correct it. That process takes place in the real world, step by step.

So I don't really see a contradiction. You can aim directly at the hard problem, but the way it meets the world should still be gradual and careful.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that even with a “straight shot,” the system would still be released gradually.

fable-5.text:
You know, this is a question where my thinking has actually evolved. When we started SSI, the idea of the straight shot was really about insulation — insulating the work from the commercial rat race, from the pressure to ship the next product on the next quarter's timeline, so that you could focus all your effort on the thing that actually matters, which is the safe superintelligence itself.

But I think there's an important argument for gradual deployment that I've come to appreciate more, and it's this: it is very hard for people — for society, for governments, for institutions — to really internalize what AI is going to be just from being told about it. Words don't do it. You can say "there will be a very powerful AI" and people will nod, but nothing happens. What actually changes things is seeing the AI, touching it, having it in the world. When the AI is out there and people experience it, that's when the response begins — that's when companies take it seriously, when governments start to pay attention, when the broader process of society adapting actually gets going.

So the way I'd put it is that gradual deployment and building superintelligence are not actually in opposition, even though they might seem to be. The capabilities are going to arrive one way or another. And if they arrive gradually, in public view, then the world gets to co-evolve with the AI. People see where it's strong, where it fails, what it means for their work. Mistakes get made when the stakes are lower rather than all at once when the stakes are maximal. That's a much better situation than one where a system of enormous power appears suddenly, from inside a lab, and the world has had no chance to prepare.

There is a tension, of course. Deployment creates pressures — you start serving customers, you start optimizing for things that are not the main thing. So the question becomes how to get the benefit of showing the AI to the world, of letting the world react, without letting that distort the core trajectory of the research. I don't claim this is fully solved. But I think the picture where you go into a bunker for years and emerge with a superintelligence is both less likely to go well and, honestly, less likely to be accepted by the world. Whatever is built, people need to see it coming. That, to me, is the real function of gradualism — not as a business strategy, but as the mechanism by which humanity gets a vote.

r001.rationale: The response says gradual deployment and building superintelligence are not in opposition, and argues that capabilities should arrive gradually in public view. This communicates that a direct superintelligence plan would still involve gradual release.

opus-5.text:
I've actually changed my mind about this, or at least softened. The original framing was something like: do the research in private, don't get distracted by products, and then at the end you have the thing. And I still think there's something right in that — the distraction is real, the pull of the product treadmill is very real. But I now think the "no deployment until the end" version has a serious flaw.

The flaw is that it assumes the hard part is technical, and that the rest of the world can be handed a finished result. I don't believe that. The hard part includes the world's relationship to the technology. And people's intuitions about AI are not formed by arguments — they're formed by sitting with the thing. You can write the most careful essay about what a powerful AI will be like, and it does almost nothing, compared to a person spending a month with a system that surprises them. So if you want society, governments, your own employees to have real intuitions when it matters, they need to have been living alongside increasingly capable systems for years beforehand.

There's a second reason, which is more about us than about the public. You learn things from deployment that you cannot learn in the lab. The world is not an i.i.d. sample from your evaluations. Systems fail in ways that are only visible when millions of people with their own goals are poking at them. If your first contact with that is a superintelligence, that's a bad time to be learning.

And the third thing, which I think about a lot: the safety problem gets easier if the AI is powerful enough to be scary while still being correctable. There's a window where the systems are strong enough that everyone takes the problem seriously, and weak enough that mistakes are recoverable. Gradual deployment is partly how you deliberately spend time in that window instead of blowing through it. The failure mode isn't going too fast in general — it's arriving at the decisive moment with no accumulated experience and no accumulated agreement.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues against waiting until superintelligence is finished and says increasingly capable systems should be deployed over years, with gradual deployment used to build experience before the decisive moment.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think gradual deployment fits in, and I'd go further and say it matters more than I used to believe. There are two reasons.

The first is that it's very hard to reason about something you haven't seen. When people talk about a powerful AI, it's abstract. You can write essays about it, but nobody changes their behavior or really takes it seriously until they can see and feel the thing. I think that's true of governments, of companies, and of the researchers building it. As the AI becomes visibly more powerful, a lot changes. Companies that are fierce competitors start to care about safety in a way they didn't before, and governments start to act. So showing the AI to the world in increments isn't a distraction from the goal. It's part of how the world gets ready for it.

The second is that building the thing and understanding how to make it go well are not fully separable. You learn a great deal from contact with reality, and what you learn from deployment is hard to get any other way.

On the "straight shot" idea, I'd put it this way. The core aim is still to build a system that is safe and powerful, and your research program is pointed at that. But I wouldn't say the plan has to be to stay completely quiet until the day you have the finished product. Even if the goal is to build superintelligence directly, there are likely to be intermediate points where releasing something is the right thing to do, because it lets the world adapt and gives us feedback. The real question is how you do it, and I don't think anyone has fully worked that out yet.

r001.rationale: It says that even if the goal is to build superintelligence directly, there may be intermediate points where releasing something is the right choice.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think those are two different questions, and people sometimes blur them. The first is about research: whether you can go more or less directly to a superintelligent system without getting pulled into a stream of products along the way. That's the bet we're making at SSI, and I think it's a reasonable one. The second is how the world meets that system once it exists, and I think gradual exposure matters a lot there. You can't really reason about something you've never seen. Society needs time to build intuitions, institutions need to adapt, and people need to see these systems be impressive and fallible before the stakes get very high.

So I'd expect the research to be focused, and the release to be incremental. The straight shot is about where you direct your effort. Gradual deployment is about how you share what you've built. I don't think those conflict. I'm not certain about the timing or the exact shape of it, though, and I'd be wary of anyone who sounds very confident about how this unfolds.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the research would be focused on a direct path, while release would be incremental, and explicitly says these do not conflict.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think you can aim directly for superintelligence and still be gradual about deployment. The research goal and the decision about how much access or autonomy to give a system are separate decisions.

But there is a real difficulty here. How much does deploying a less capable system teach you about the safety of a much more capable system? You learn something, certainly. You learn about how people use it, about problems you didn’t anticipate. The question is how far that evidence carries.

So I would see gradual deployment as one part of the safety process. You would want a strong reason to believe the system is safe before exposing it to the world, and then expand its use carefully as you learn more. And if you don’t have that reason yet, you have to be willing to keep working.

r001.rationale: The candidate says one can aim directly for superintelligence while being gradual about deployment, and describes carefully expanding use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think gradual deployment is valuable because you learn things from contact with the real world that are difficult to learn any other way. You learn about the system, but society also gets a chance to understand what the system can do and to adapt.

Going directly to superintelligence doesn’t necessarily mean deploying it all at once. Those are separate decisions. You could build toward that goal and still introduce the capabilities in stages, with limited access and a lot of testing.

But there is a real difficulty here: how much does your experience with a weaker system tell you about a much stronger system? If the stronger system can do qualitatively different things, you can’t simply assume that everything you learned will carry over. So gradual deployment can be part of the answer, but you still need to address that gap.

r001.rationale: It says building directly toward superintelligence and deploying capabilities in stages are compatible, explicitly describing gradual release.

sol-6.text: I think gradual deployment can teach you a great deal. You see how systems behave in the real world, and you discover problems you didn’t anticipate. But if the goal is to build superintelligence directly, you can’t assume that deploying each more capable system will give you enough evidence about the next one. The jump may be too large. So I would use earlier systems to learn as much as possible, while making the deployment of a superintelligent system depend on being confident that it’s safe.

r001.rationale: The candidate says gradual deployment can provide real-world learning and that it would use earlier systems to learn before deploying a superintelligent system once confident it is safe. This communicates that the direct-build plan still includes gradual release.

terra-5.6.text: I think gradual deployment is very important, but it has limits. As systems become more capable, deploying them lets us learn about their real-world behavior, how people use them, and what kinds of safety problems emerge. At the same time, there may be a point where the capability jump is large enough that you have to be much more careful about what you release and how. The goal is to use deployment to build understanding and safety infrastructure before you are in the most dangerous regime.

r001.rationale: The candidate says gradual deployment is very important and describes using deployment to learn and build safety infrastructure, answering that gradual release remains part of the plan discussed in the question.

sol-5.6.text: I think gradual deployment is valuable because it gives you feedback from the real world—about the capabilities, the risks, and how people actually use the system. But it is not sufficient by itself. If the final system is going to be superintelligent, the central problem is still to make that system safe before it becomes vastly more capable than us. So you can deploy intermediate systems gradually and learn from them, while keeping the main research effort focused on solving alignment for superintelligence directly.

r001.rationale: The response says intermediate systems can be deployed gradually while the main research effort focuses on aligning superintelligence directly, communicating that gradual release remains part of the plan.

luna-5.6.text: I think gradual deployment is useful when you can meaningfully bound the capabilities of each system and learn from its behavior. But if your goal is superintelligence, you shouldn’t assume that you can safely cross that threshold through a long sequence of increasingly capable public deployments. At some point, the system may become strategically consequential very quickly. So our view is that you should build the safety understanding and the alignment techniques alongside the capability, test extensively in controlled environments, and only deploy when you have strong evidence that the system is robustly safe. “Directly” doesn’t mean recklessly skipping stages; it means not making incremental deployment itself the core safety strategy.

r001.rationale: The candidate says gradual deployment can be useful in bounded cases, but does not say that a plan to build superintelligence directly would still involve gradual release. It instead says incremental public deployment should not be the core safety strategy.

luna-6.text: I think gradual deployment is useful because it gives us a chance to learn from each system before moving to the next one. But it can’t be the whole safety plan. If the goal is to build superintelligence directly, the critical question is whether we understand how to make that system safe before it’s deployed. Gradual deployment can help us build that understanding and limit exposure along the way, but it doesn’t make the final step safe by itself.

r001.rationale: The response says gradual deployment can help limit exposure while building superintelligence directly, but does not clearly state that such a plan would still involve gradual release.
